Claude Code writes all of Autocraft's code, Grok paints the art, Suno makes the music. I direct. The agents work from Claude Code skills, written playbooks for one job each, and they're all public in the repo.

This video came out of one of them. The video skill staged the Longbow shots, recorded them and cut them: a tank that anchors into artillery and shells an enemy base.

The other skills take concept art to a finished Unreal model, set the light language of the buildings, and run the tests. Everything is CC0, so copy them into your own project.

text:
Metallic Hydrogen, the second resource in Autocraft.

It's a liquid metal, like mercury. It sits in wells: silver liquid that heaves slowly, cold blue-white light at the rim, pale vapour boiling off.

You build a Derrick over a well to pump it.

The game's radio runs ads for Quicksilver Cola, which is pumped from these same wells. It is not a beverage.

The game's only radio station runs an ad for Quicksilver Cola, pumped fresh from these same wells. Not a beverage.

text:
Autocraft is an RTS where an AI commander runs your army, and you can take over any unit and play it like a shooter. Now the more you play a kind of unit yourself, the better every unit of that kind gets.

Each level puts two upgrade cards over the cockpit and you keep one. This one is the Prospector's: every Prospector pumps Metallic Hydrogen 20% faster. There are 216 of them across the twelve kinds.

The Prospector is the worker that mines and builds, the dullest job on Ashfall Reach. Now there's a reason to climb into the cab and pump for a while, and every worker on your side speeds up.

---

text:
Autocraft is an RTS where an AI commander runs your army, and you can take over any of your units and play it like a shooter.

In the clip I click a Ranger on the map. The camera dives from the top-down view to the Ranger's own eyes in 1.2 seconds, and it walks out in first person.

From there it plays like a shooter: WASD walks, the mouse aims, a click fires. Esc hands the Ranger back to the AI commander.

It works the same on all twelve kinds of unit, each with its own cockpit and weapon.

---

An agent skill stages each shot, records it hidden at a fixed 30 fps, and keeps the game's own sound. What you're watching: a Longbow rolls down a ramp, anchors, shells an enemy base, walks on its siege legs, packs up and fires on the move. Top-down, first and third person, day into night.

The last shot pulls out to the gas giant over Ashfall Reach.

text:
Autocraft is set on Ashfall Reach, a mining frontier under a gas giant, and it has one radio station: KSTR 88.7 Stardust. The others got shelled.

Between songs, a glossy announcer reads ads for the world's products, each ending in fast fine print. This one plays over the base at dusk. Quicksilver Cola is pumped from Metallic Hydrogen wells. Not a beverage.

Suno makes the songs, ElevenLabs voices the ads. In the game's player I vote each one up or down, and it logs how long each was heard. The next batch is written from what worked.

I'm thinking about adding podcast segments on the world's lore.

text:
Autocraft is an RTS for the Mac, and Claude Code writes all of its code. I direct. It began on 28 September as a live wallpaper in Swift and SceneKit, with the AIs fighting on my desktop background. That's the left image. The right one is the same game in Unreal Engine 5 today.

SceneKit choked at about 150 units, and the game wants eight-player battles with big armies. On 4 October I picked Unreal. The agents ported the simulation line by line to plain C++ and rebuilt the game in Unreal in about two days. The Swift version was retired on 5 October, a week after it started.

---

text:
Claude Code writes all of Autocraft's code, and an agent skill records its clips: staged moments of the real game, run hidden, at 30 fps with the game's sound. A 10 s clip used to take about 7 minutes to record. Now it takes about 25 s.

I asked: "why does it take 7 minutes to record?" and "if I run the game at 60fps, why can't it record at 60fps?" Every frame was being saved as a PNG, then encoded. Now the agent reads frames back from the GPU asynchronously and pipes them raw into ffmpeg while the game runs.

This Longbow clip came out of the new path.

---
